paras: The attempted lynching of George Starkweather took place on 12 April 1888, when a crowd of citizens seized the 60-year-old wood chopper from a justice's office in Pennsylvania and put a rope around his neck. A sheriff's posse rescued him and took him to the jail at Garland. Papers across the country carried the Titusville wire dispatch, several under headlines regretting that he had escaped.

Starkweather lived near Grand Valley, Pennsylvania, and was the father of eleven children. On 11 April he was arrested, charged with raping his eldest child, a daughter aged 15, and his wife was named as the accuser.

At a hearing before a justice the next day, according to the dispatch, it was "developed" that he had abused the girl since she was 12, under threats of death if she told anyone. After the daughter's testimony, "the indignant citizens" seized Starkweather, dragged him from the justice's office and placed a rope around his neck. A sheriff's posse arrived at that point, rescued him and removed him to Garland jail "for safety." The reports give no number for the crowd and name none of its members or the officers.
No report of arrests among the crowd, or of Starkweather's later trial or sentence, appears in the coverage.

All of the coverage traces to a single dispatch from Titusville, which papers in Washington, St. Paul, Springfield, Ohio, Rock Island, Maysville and Yankton printed on 13 and 14 April 1888 with only small changes. Editors chose headlines that sided with the crowd: the St. Paul Daily Globe ran "Should Have Been Lynched," the Springfield Daily Republic "He Deserved Lynching," and the Maysville Evening Bulletin "Justice Defeated." The Press and Daily Dakotaian of Yankton headed it "An Incestuous Beast" and blamed "the Inopportune Arrival of a Blundering Sheriff's Posse," while the National Republican called him "a Wretch Who Unfortunately Escaped Lynching."

Other papers ran the story without such comment, as the Evening Star's brief "A Brutal Father Narrowly Escapes Lynching" and a one-sentence item in the Indiana State Sentinel's news column on 18 April. None of the reports mentioned the race of Starkweather or of the crowd.

Copies differ on the dates because editors reworded the dispatch: the April 12 versions say he was arrested "yesterday" and attacked "to-day," and the Rock Island and Maysville versions give Wednesday and Thursday, which agree. The Yankton paper alone says he was arrested on Thursday, and the Springfield paper places the arrest the day before an April 13 dateline.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Starkweather
bases: A crowd of citizens seized an accused man from a justice's office and put a rope around his neck before a sheriff's posse rescued him, an attempted lynching (A1, A2).

Starkweather was not killed: a sheriff's posse rescued him after 'indignant citizens' put a rope around his neck, so this was an attempt; the crowd acted without authority on a rape and incest charge, but its size is not given (A1, A5).
Every report is a copy of one Titusville, Pa., wire dispatch, reworded only in its dates and headlines; no local paper or follow-up was found (A1, A5, A8).

accounts.label: Titusville wire report
accounts.gist: After the daughter's testimony at the hearing, citizens seized Starkweather from the justice's office and had a rope around his neck when a sheriff's posse rescued him and took him to Garland jail.

framing.detail: Headlines endorsed the attempt or lamented its failure: 'Should Have Been Lynched' (St. Paul), 'He Deserved Lynching' (Springfield), 'Justice Defeated' (Maysville), 'The Inopportune Arrival of a Blundering Sheriff's Posse' (Yankton), and 'a Wretch Who Unfortunately Escaped Lynching' (Washington).
The Evening Star and the Indiana State Sentinel ran the story as a brief news item without comment beyond 'A Brutal Father'.

versions.value: Arrested 'yesterday' (11 April) and attempt 'to-day' (12 April), dateline April 12

conflicts.note: The April 12 copies are the earliest; Wednesday/Thursday agrees with them (12 April 1888 was a Thursday). The Yankton and Springfield wordings come from editors redating the dispatch.
